Utility software is a group of small programs that each carry out one task to help the operating system keep the computer running well. They include the disk defragmenter, the task scheduler, backup and restore tools and antivirus software. To understand defragmentation, think about how files are saved. The operating system splits a file into blocks and puts each block in any free space on the disk. As files are saved and deleted over months, the free space ends up as lots of small gaps spread around the disk.
Makes sense. Keep going.

A large new file may then be split into pieces stored in different places. This is called file fragmentation. On a hard disk drive, the read/write head has to keep jumping around to collect every piece, which slows the computer down. A defragmenter moves the pieces so each file is stored in one continuous area and the free space is grouped together. Solid-state drives have no moving parts, so they gain nothing from this.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Task scheduling means dividing the processor's time between several tasks so the system is used as efficiently as possible. In a multi-user system, the scheduler uses the round robin method. The processor works on a task from the first computer for a short time slice, then moves to the second, then the third, and after the last one it goes back to the start. Because each slice is tiny and the processor is very fast, everybody feels that they have the computer to themselves.
Got it. Keep going.

The word task scheduler is also used for the utility that runs jobs automatically at a planned time or when something happens. For example, a school's network manager might schedule a full virus scan every Friday evening, a backup at two in the morning and updates to install when computers shut down. The jobs run when nobody is using the system, so work is not interrupted, and they are never forgotten.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A backup is a copy of data stored separately from the original so that it can be used if the original is lost or damaged. Data can be lost when a hard disk fails, when a virus or ransomware attacks, when someone deletes a file by mistake, or when a fire or flood destroys a building. For a hospital, a bank or a school, losing records could be disastrous. Backups should be kept off-site or in the cloud, somewhere secure, so a single disaster cannot destroy both copies.
Okay. Keep going.

A full backup copies all the data, which takes a long time and a lot of space. An incremental backup only copies data that has changed since the last backup, so it is much quicker. Many organisations run a full backup once a week and incremental backups on the other nights, scheduled overnight when the network is quiet. Restoring means copying the backed-up data back onto the system to return it to its earlier state.
Go on.

A virus is a harmful program that attaches itself to a file. When the file is opened, the virus runs and spreads to other files and to other computers on a network or the internet. Viruses can damage or delete data, stop a computer from starting up and slow it down. Antivirus software protects against them. It scans the files on the computer's internal drive and on any connected storage, as well as data arriving through emails and downloads.
Right. Keep going.

It compares what it finds against a database of known virus signatures, which are patterns of code belonging to each virus. Many programs also look for suspicious behaviour that might come from a brand-new virus. When it finds a threat, the software removes it, repairs the file or moves it into quarantine so it cannot run. Because new viruses appear all the time, the signature database must be updated regularly, otherwise the newest threats will slip through undetected.

Utility software?
A program that carries out one specific task to help the operating system maintain, protect or speed up the computer, e dot g. defragmenter, task scheduler, backup, antivirus.
File fragmentation?
When a file's data blocks are stored in separate, non-adjacent places on a disk because there is not enough continuous free space.
Disk defragmenter?
A utility that rearranges the fragments of files on a disk so each file is stored in continuous blocks and free space is grouped together, speeding up file access.
Task scheduler?
A utility that shares processor time between tasks (e dot g. round robin) and runs jobs such as backups, virus scans or updates automatically at set times.
Round robin?
A scheduling method in which each task or user is given a time slice of the processor in turn, returning to the first after the last.
Backup?
A copy of data stored separately, preferably off-site, so it can be restored if the original is lost or damaged.
